abstract: In Part I, a gamma friction that follows theta velocity produced theta gamma phase amplitude coupling (PAC) whose strength is a closed-form function of one dimensionless number, kappa;. Here we ask when this coupling destabilizes the gamma oscillator. The friction on gamma is negative during part of every theta cycle, yet gamma stays bounded: as long as it keeps oscillating, the energy gained while theta rises is returned while theta falls, and Liouville' sformula fixes the growth over a theta cycle at the baseline decay, whatever the coupling. Instability arises only in rare large theta cycles in which the friction exceeds critical damping, so that gamma stops oscillating and the gain is no longer returned. The typical trajectory becomes unstable when such cycles, about one in a hundred, outweigh the decay in all the others. This gives a boundary g* {sigma}x = 10, where {sigma}x is the typical theta amplitude set by the fluctuation dissipation theorem; the prediction agrees with a direct Lyapunov scan to within 6% for damping ratios from 0.0005 to 0.0055. The distance to the boundary is set by the same number kappa that sets the PAC strength, so that stronger PAC means closer proximity to instability. The mean-square boundary lies far lower but is set by events of negligible probability. Stimulating theta at or below its own frequency raises gamma energy and PAC and can drive giant gamma bursts or divergence, but no self-sustained activity, suggesting that a transition to seizure requires memory.
